title: Sowing chard microgreens
subtitle: How to prepare and sow a chard microgreen tray, including the cluster-separation step
excerpt: Chard seed is a corky multi-germ cluster that germinates as a group. Rubbing the clusters between your palms before sowing partially separates them, giving more even coverage. The rest of the sowing process is standard: fill, scatter at 20 to 25 g per tray, press, blackout.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: A seed structure where multiple seeds are fused together in a corky outer layer. Beetroot and chard both produce multi-germ clusters; when sown, each cluster can germinate as a group, producing several shoots in close proximity. Partially separating the cluster before sowing gives more even distribution across the tray.

The period immediately after sowing when a second tray is stacked on top, blocking light from the sown tray. In darkness, germinating seeds direct energy into pushing the shoot upward rather than greening. For chard, expect three to four days before the shoots are ready to move to light.

content.text: Chard seed differs from small round brassica seeds: each piece is a corky cluster containing multiple seeds. Sowing chard clusters without preparation produces dense clumps of seedlings surrounded by bare patches. A quick cluster-separation step before sowing distributes the seedlings more evenly.
One 25 cm × 25 cm growing tray. A second tray for the blackout cover. Seed compost. Chard seed: 20 to 25 g per tray. A flat piece of card or the base of the second tray for pressing.

Step 1: separate the seed clusters. Take the chard seed and rub a small handful between your palms with light friction. This breaks the outer corky layer into smaller fragments without destroying the inner seeds.
do not need to be perfectly separated; partial breaking is sufficient to improve distribution. Some clusters will still remain as a group but with smaller fragments, which space out better.
Step 2: pre-dampen seed compost and fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim. Level the surface.

Step 3: scatter the rubbed seed clusters at 20 to 25 g per tray. The fragmented clusters are bulkier than round brassica seed; scatter from 15 cm above the tray surface, distributing in sections across the tray.
Step 4: press firmly to ensure good contact with the medium beneath.
: cover with the second tray and a light weight. Chard germinates in three to four days. Remove the cover when the majority of shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common sowing-stage problems with chard microgreens.

items.symptom: Clumped seedlings in groups with bare patches between them
items.cause: Seed clusters not separated before sowing.
items.fix: Rub more firmly between the palms on the next attempt. Some clustering is unavoidable, but smaller clusters give much better tray coverage.

items.symptom: Germination much slower than expected — day 6 and still no shoots
items.fix: Warm the room above 16°C. Check the medium moisture by pressing a finger to the surface; it should feel damp but not wet. Bottom-water if it feels dry.
